item.title: @testingcatalog：谷歌推出名为Loop的新型自适应人工智能代理，旨在实现自主协同工作与任务管理
item.description:
Google recently announced Loop, its new self-improving AI agent that can autonomously work toward a given goal.

Loop is internally called Jitro; interestingly, that was the exact name for Jules v2.

Here is how it works 👀

1. Users start creating a Workspace by connecting it to a selected Github project and adding basic information.

2. Users can create loops manually or select ones that are already predefined (ex., Harden Application Security)

"Custom Loops" can be created via a prompt or by manually filling in the Loop title, icon, and objective.

> "Loops are mid- to long-term objectives for Stitch Loop to continuously work toward. They can range from highly specific to broad, but should always be something code can achieve," says the description.

3. Users can connect additional context in the form of Integrations, Files, Links, or additional repositories.

More than 100 integrations are available there, including services like Jira, Linear, Datadog, Sentry, Notion, Snowflake, Salesforce, Intercom, Discord, Slack, Figma, and many others.

Custom MCPs are supported as well.

4. After creating a workspace, Loop will start digging into your project details and generate its own Skills about the product and product metrics.

These Skills will live in a separate tab and can be edited in the UI in Markdown.

5. When the Workspace is ready, Loop will suggest metrics and goals based on its own research. Users can convert these suggestions into loops right away.

When a Loop is created, it appears as a running process in the main UI.

6. When a Loop is finished, users will see a list of suggestions for every loop, along with a number associated with a target metric and progress status.

Example Loop:
- Goal - Scale Telegram community contributions.
- KPIs - community members, registered contributors, active members.

A high-level goal would be broken down into sub-KPIs. When users open a dedicated Loop page, all these KPIs will be visible on the dashboard.

Below, Users will see a list of Tasks, Skills, and Activity tabs.

Example Task:
- Telegram channel lacks discussion threads and a dedicated bot.

Each task has a detailed description, labels, and the date when it was updated. Below, users will see tabs for Solutions, Activity, and Evidence.

Activity appears as a summary describing what happened, what was done, and the general Timeline.

Evidence contains links to where Loop pulled the context behind this Task. In my example case, it refers to the TestingCatalog website and the Telegram channel from which it pulled all the numbers.

Example Solution:
- Dedicated Telegram Bot API intake bot with editorial triage webhook (implementation task).

This task is an implementation task that has a clear description, Impact, scope, and Risk labeled.

Users can start the task right from this page to begin solution development via Gemini.

When the task is done, users can review its progress and status and monitor its impact on production by pulling updated metrics and KPIs after the release.

What does all this mean? 🤯

Loop follows how "Product work" is done at Google, a model many other companies also use.

Every Workspace in Loop is equivalent to a scope that is normally handled by a complete product engineering team.

It is no longer a place where users play the role of engineering lead and product lead, orchestrating AI agents.

It is a place where the user plays the role of a senior manager managing several engineering teams, which is a big shift on its own.

We are slowly moving towards autonomous AI organizations. One management layer at a time.

I expect it will still take until 2027 for labs to develop the products and models needed to make substantial progress in this area (assuming AI continues to advance in a semi-regulated format as it is now).

Monitoring 🍿

item.title: @giffmana：新版Gemini模型Neon在代码生成与数据集可视化测试中表现优异
item.description:
ok, I have to agree, on first try, Neon seems much better than previous Gemini models, I'll very cautiously congratulate the team :)

I did a side-by-side test of Opus5.5, Muse Wonder Full, Sol 6.2, and Neon (All on high or more). One "dumb" prompt to generate a dataset viewer.

Result: they all functionally nailed the task, but Neon actually made the (subjectively) "nicest" one!

My prompt, in an empty folder, and no further details or interaction from me:

> So look, there is the fine-vision dataset on huggingface which is a big mix of VLM datasets. In there, there's the coco_color or coco_colors dataset. Please download it (if it's not many gigs, otherwise just download a subset), and make an interactive webpage I can run locally which shows stats about it and then an example viewer, showing the image and question/answer pair(s). Show examples on a grid I can scroll through, and also, for each example, add a button "to the back" that just pushes this example all the way to the back of the grid. I want to basically browse through it and get the nice examples to the front so I can make a funny screenshog.

END OF PROMPT

- Time taken: Sol 6min29s < Neon 6min37s < Muse 9min15s < Opus 15min7s
- Downloaded: Opus+Neon = 1 shard (490mb/5.6k ex), Muse+Sol = 300 examples (~20mb)
- Needs server? Opus+Sol = no, Muse+Neon = yes. I prefer no.

They all made a good functional viewer that fulfils all my desires. From the look, I'd say Opus+Muse boring, Sol+Neon nice. They all show at least some basic stats at the top, in these now clear-ai-slop chips.

However, what set Neon apart here, is that it seems to really want to understand and show the data structure. It chose nice ways to show (and allow filtering by) the properties. It notices and highlihgts quirks in the dataset. Unfortunately, the "progress-bar thingy" that's supposed to visualize % is broken. Of course fixed in one prompt.

Also, Neon and Opus realized the data is all about colors and got the idea to insert these color-dots inside the labels for easier reading. Muse and Sol only show plain text. My past self who did this manually, usually made the font in the color, which none of the 4 decided to do.

So yeah, I have bashed Gemini a lot in the past, but Neon indeed seems good now, congrats to the team!

Also, this dataset is pretty bad, don't use it lol

Reminder: racing to self-improve the verifiable subset of capabilities, which is what AI companies are currently doing, _decreases_ the window of time that they have to convert into sustainable businesses and do the boring work of turning value creation into value capture.

(Of course, their bet is that progress in verifiable tasks will somehow yield progress on unverifiable tasks. We'll see.)

@random_walker：As AI labs race toward Recursive Self Improvement, there’s a possibility that what they are actually racing toward is Recursive Self Extinction — of their business model. Here’s my reasoning.

1. Progress on verifiable tasks continues. In particular, improving the cost efficiency of existing capabilities is a highly verifiable task. For the past few years, cost per equivalent capability has dropped by at least 10x per year. I think this progress will be sustained for a few more years, and even accelerate as labs use AI more and more heavily for AI research in the pursuit of RSI. There is of course a ceiling to efficiency improvements, but I don’t think we’re close to that ceiling.

2. Progress on most unverifiable tasks remains frustratingly hard. AI inherits the same limitations (ambiguous success criteria, slow and noisy feedback) that limit human performance at tasks ranging from writing to governance. The optimization paradigm generally doesn’t result in superhuman capabilities on such tasks, because whatever proxy you optimize for gets Goodharted. item.title: @omarsar0：最新研究探讨大模型控制框架作为组合泛化器的作用及对模型能力的提升
item.description:
Highly recommended read. Learn to build your own harness, folks.

My belief—and that of many fully AI-native builders and companies—is that harnesses remain largely underexplored.

Research shows a huge edge in custom harnesses.

But little is known about why.

Alex and colleagues have been exploring this direction and have noted that harnesses can act as compositional generalizers.

In other words, harnesses can push LLMs further (with stronger generalization effects) through existing LLM capabilities.

Harnesses like RLMs are a good recent example, with abstractions that unlock this.

I have recently started seeing success in post-training used to co-evolve harnesses and models. I think this could explain why this is happening, but more research is needed to understand this better.

I have experienced this with a variant of dynamic workflows I have implemented in my meta harness.

@a1zhang：Harnesses used to be a crutch for weak LLMs. In 2026 and onward, with stronger models, harnesses now offer a mechanism for composing an LLM’s existing and new capabilities to generalize well beyond their training environments.

In our new paper, LM Harnesses are Compositional Generalizers, we explore how various harness abstractions enable LM systems to generalize over task length, task strategies, recursive task depth, and more through composing existing LLM capabilities. These abstractions provide a means for more data-efficient training, especially over long tasks, by keeping trajectories locally in-distribution (LID) — i.e., shaping all individual LLM calls to be in-distribution.

For tasks that take a very long time to roll out, this implies that we can even perform surrogate harness training, meaning we train an individual LLM call instead of doing the very long harness rollout, using purely synthetic tasks, with fake tool calls + sub-agents!

A common idea floating around is that LLMs will absorb harnesses and make them obsolete. We disagree, and argue that we haven’t sufficiently explored what harnesses can provide.

The full paper, logs, codebase, and data are available: https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2611.harness-cg

item.title: @Thom_Wolf：Hugging Face推出专用内容分发网络以应对人工智能大模型和数据集的下载需求
item.description:
AI downloads broke the usual CDN model

Since this summer, we're running our own CDN at Hugging Face. It's shipping almost 1 exabyte per month, which means, in practice, about 420 GB every second, through 80,000 requests per second.

Why did we need to build our own?

Well, CDNs were designed to ship many small web files to many people. AI downloads are pretty different: it's a few enormous files, a significant part of them pulled by machines.

This changes a lot of design assumptions.

You're not caching small objects close to users in hundreds of cities anymore: these users are for a big part GPU clusters sitting in a handful of cloud regions.

And a cached web page is useful to 1,000 visitors, while a cached 1,000 GB model is useful to far fewer clients, but each one wants all of it, immediately.

So we've built our own CDN, with caches adapted to massive objects, able to handle release-day mega-floods and multiple giant datasets and trending models being pulled at once.

On 17 Nov Harvey co-founder Gabe Pereyra wrote that about 30 AI agents, with one human director approving decisions, wrote a Word-compatible editor in three weeks. That is over 1 million lines of code, more than 7,000 commits and 14,600 tests. He also wrote that Cognition builds its Android app with one Devin bot managing other Devins and no engineers.

X read this next to a DeepMind essay which argues that once AI agents coordinate with each other past a threshold, concentration, employment and wages change abruptly. The viral conclusion is that agents are about to replace whole firms.

Anyone who uses coding agents heavily expected results like Harvey's. Both projects rebuild a product that already exists. Harvey's agents checked their editor against Word, and Cognition's agents check the Android app against the existing iOS app. The existing product defines the correct result for every change, so the agents can test their own work and one human director is enough. One Harvey release checked about 12.8 million edits for corruption.

The DeepMind essay itself says current AI systems coordinate poorly in practice. These two teams worked because an existing product had already specified the target.

Any AI-native startup can do this with the same models, so I expect it to be commoditized.

As a heavy user of agents, the question I care about more is what they still cannot do. These are the tasks where I cannot simply tell the agents what I want and get the finished result back. There are still many of them. Work on a new product with no existing reference is one, because there is nothing to test each change against.

Those tasks are where a startup's competitive edge will come from. Building an editor or an Android app with agents will not set a company apart.

item.description:
The test of the Jensen story is what Nvidia does about open weights next

Jensen Huang resigned from $NVDA on 11 Nov after a spy story the Justice Department says it has reached no conclusion on. That news is old. The live question is whether his open-weight stance made him a target.

The usual rebuttal is that Nvidia is buying about $10B of Anthropic ($ANT) stock, so Nvidia and the frontier labs are on the same side. We don't blindly accept that. The stake aligns Nvidia, the company, with Anthropic. It says nothing about Jensen, who was the most vocal champion of open-weight models and put Nvidia's balance sheet behind US open-model labs such as Reflection and Thinking Machines.

ANT's own prospectus names open-weight models as a source of pricing pressure. A Nvidia that holds $10B of ANT and no longer has Jensen has a reason to stop funding that pressure.

Look at who carries weight in Washington. Anthropic spent $5.6M on federal lobbying in 2026 through September. Nvidia spent $4.69M and OpenAI just under $3.8M. A lab outspent the company at the centre of chip policy. We think Nvidia's real influence in Washington was Jensen himself, and that has gone.

No reporting ties any lab to his exit and we have no evidence of it. What Nvidia does next on open weights will show whether the concern is justified.

Over the next few months we are watching three things:

• Whether the open-model deals Nvidia was expected to join or lead still close.
• What the permanent CEO says about open weights.
• Whether Nvidia's pitch moves from enterprises running their own models to serving Anthropic and OpenAI.

If Nvidia keeps backing open weights, the suspicion weakens. If it retreats, the suspicion hardens.

A retreat would also be poor strategy. ANT's firm commitments for $GOOGL TPUs exceed $280B. Its Nvidia GPU contracts run up to about $200B, and the largest becomes cancellable on 90 days' notice from early 2027. Google sells Anthropic the chips, is buying about $10B of ANT stock itself and competes with Gemini. Nvidia's $10B is also small next to what its rivals hold: Google and Amazon together own about 28% of Anthropic, worth roughly $300B at the IPO price.

Open weights spread Nvidia's demand across a broad base of enterprises that run their own models. Frontier labs have the most alternatives because they are big enough to design their own chips or split orders across suppliers: Google builds its TPUs in-house, OpenAI is designing accelerators with Broadcom, and Anthropic buys Google TPUs, Amazon Trainium and AMD GPUs alongside Nvidia. If Nvidia neglects its open-weight enterprise customers to lean on a few frontier labs, it ends up depending on customers such as Anthropic that are also buying Google's TPUs, and that helps Google.

item.title: @convequity：谷歌发布Gemini 4 Neon并在编码基准测试中排名靠前
item.description:
Gemini 4 Neon ranks first on coding benchmarks. After testing the Gemini 4 models, I would not replace Opus with them for engineering work

Google ($GOOGL) launched Gemini 4 Neon on 18 Nov at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. It ranks first on the most-cited independent coding-agent index with a score of 58.6, and X is arguing whether it dethrones Claude.

Neon is a real step up for Google. It is far better than Gemini 3.8 Flash, and for the previous few quarters Google users only had a Flash-tier model to work with. Its writing is very impressive, and so is its world knowledge.

In my testing currently, Gemini 4 behaves more like GPT-6.2 Astra than like Opus in engineering work. I see the same two problems I see with Astra. It over-engineers, which means it builds more than the task asked for. And it follows the instructions or the agent guide to the letter without using its own judgment, so it can be single-minded in a way that does not look intelligent.

Benchmarks do not capture this. Google's own launch blog shows how much a coding score depends on the setup. On the SWE-sweep test, the same Neon model scores 12.8% in a basic harness and 39.0% inside Antigravity, Google's own agent product.

A benchmark score records whether the task was completed in that setup. It does not record whether the model built only what was needed, or whether it knew when to depart from its instructions. I call that taste, and we need a benchmark or some other way to verify it.

I have not seen a dramatic take-up in Gemini usage or an oversubscribed Antigravity, and I think this is the reason.

OpenAI and Google have the compute and the know-how to train a larger model and reach the top tier of the benchmarks. In daily use their models are still not comparable to Anthropic's. Anthropic is now public as $ANT, and I expect its competitive position to stay strong for the next two quarters.

item.title: @convequity：美国关于海外GPU访问的新规或将推低GPU租赁价格并影响云厂商
item.description:
The new US rule on Chinese access to overseas GPUs could push GPU rental prices down. That hurts GPU cloud companies and helps Anthropic

The US Commerce Department rule that took effect on 19 Nov requires a US licence to transfer advanced GPUs to any data centre in the world that provides more than a set amount of compute to companies headquartered in China. The threshold is 12 million TPP, the US government's measure of chip performance, which is reportedly about 300 of the most advanced GPUs. Existing providers have 90 days to apply for a licence.

The first casualty is already visible. Datasection, a Japanese neo-cloud, meaning a company that rents out GPU capacity, cut its fiscal-year revenue guidance by 89% after a large order was cancelled. Reports say its capacity was in practice a Tencent data centre running Nvidia ($NVDA) Blackwell chips, and that it still has unpaid GPU purchase commitments.

Most of the commentary asks whether the loophole is closed. I think the bigger effect is on GPU rental prices.

The capacity that was reserved for Chinese customers still exists, and its operators still have GPU bills to pay. They have to find new buyers in a very short period, and the place to find them is the public spot market, where GPU capacity is rented at the current price instead of on a long contract. My estimate is that this capacity is 10% to 15% of global GPU cloud supply. And it can be a vast majority of the spot rental you can get for a large compute capacity which is a rare opportunity. That much capacity looking for buyers at once pushes spot prices down.

In the short term this hurts Western neo-clouds such as CoreWeave ($CRWV), IREN ($IREN) and Nebius ($NBIS), and even SpaceX. Lower spot prices reduce what they can charge for capacity that is not yet under contract.

It is good news for the buyers. Anthropic ($ANT) and other AI labs have been suffering from rising compute costs. If Anthropic locks in this capacity, its compute cost falls over the coming quarters and its gross margin improves.

I also expect open-source models to lose ground over the next two quarters. Cheaper compute and weaker open-source competition arriving together make this a very good period for Anthropic.

Watch for more guidance cuts from non-US neo-clouds before the 90-day licence window closes in mid-February 2027.

item.title: @omarsar0：Meta研究人员提出Benchmark Factory方案：通过智能体循环将内部代码变更转化为编程评测基准
item.description:
Interesting paper from Meta showing how to build coding evals from your own codebase.

(bookmark it)

Good benchmarks are hard to create, but using this method with agents looks promising.

They propose Benchmark Factory, an agent loop that turns merged internal code changes into benchmarks. It writes the query that selects tasks, runs models of known relative strength, and repairs the benchmark until it passes a set of quality checks. These checks need no per-task human labels.

To make sure the checks catch bad benchmarks, the authors fed them bad benchmarks on purpose. A benchmark that was far too easy got rejected. So did benchmarks with five different kinds of broken grading. When they scrambled which model was which, a bad benchmark slipped through at most 1.4% of the time.

On configurations never used to build them, the benchmarks ranked Claude Opus 4.7 at high effort above low effort (60.6% vs 54.4%) and GPT-5.5 above GPT-5.4 (65.8% vs 60.5%). 9 of 10 per-team comparisons agreed.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18890

item.title: @convequity：硅光子光学开关与机械开关在损耗及端口数上面临不同技术取舍
item.description:
Silicon-photonics optical switches can change paths in nanoseconds, but they lose light at every stage, and that loss can make them hard to deploy.

An optical circuit switch keeps the signal as light from end to end. $LITE's MEMS mirrors and HUBER+SUHNER's piezoelectric Polatis do this mechanically, switching in milliseconds.

Electro-optic silicon-photonics switches route light through paths on a chip and reconfigure in nanoseconds. That could let a network rearrange connections as traffic changes.

The problem is insertion loss, and it comes from keeping the light on a chip. Light loses power at the couplers where it enters and leaves the chip, along the waveguides that carry it across, and at each switching element. A switch with more ports usually needs more stages in series, and each stage leaves less power for the next, so less reaches the receiver.

Mechanical switches lose far less. A MEMS mirror or a Polatis piezoelectric actuator steers the beam through free space from the input fibre to the output fibre in one pass, with no chain of on-chip stages, so the loss stays low even at large port counts.

Amplifiers can make up the loss on the chip, as an IBM-led demonstration showed. They cannot recover data already corrupted by noise.

Our view: the switch types will coexist. We expect the choice to depend on how often a network changes its connections, port count, optical loss and cost.

item.description:
@nicbstme：I never looked at the X algorithm before today. It's open source, and they have a file called param .rs with the actual weights used to rank your “For You feed”

The most surprising thing: copying a post's link has a weight of 20. Liking it has a weight of 0.7. Copying the link is the most valuable thing you can do with a post, weighted almost 30x more than a like and 4x more than a reply.

My guess why: when you copy a link, you're about to paste it somewhere else. A group chat, Slack, an email. That's the strongest signal there is that a post is worth something, and it brings new people onto X. A like costs nothing. Sending something to a friend means you're putting your name on it.

The rest of the list tells a bit of a similar story like a reply is 5, a quote is 5, sharing by DM is 5, following the author is 4, a share is 2.1, a repost is 1, and a like is 0.7. Literally I didn’t know that repost does almost nothing.

The negatives are brutal btw a report is -234, a mute is -59, "not interested" is -53 and a block is -31.

A reply from someone you follow who follows you back gets a 15x boost. Conversations between real connections matter most (and not bots!)

Reposts don't reach strangers. A filter drops a repost for anyone who doesn't follow the reposter. A quote is a new post, so it can travel much further. Quote beats repost so you always have to add your own thoughts to a post.
